questions.subject: Botany
questions.q:
Which of the following are characteristic features of Solanaceae family ?
(a) Flowers are bisexual and actinomorphic
(b) Calyx have five sepals and are united
(c) Androecium have five stamens and are epipetalous
(d) Ovary is inferior
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
The floral features of the Solanaceae family are as follows:

Flowers are typically bisexual and actinomorphic.

The calyx consists of five sepals which are united (gamosepalous) and are often persistent.

The androecium consists of five stamens which are epipetalous (attached to the petals).

The gynoecium consists of a superior ovary, which is bicarpellary and syncarpous with a swollen placenta.

Therefore, statements (a), (b), and (c) are correct, while statement (d) is incorrect because the ovary is superior, not inferior.

Answer: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In racemose inflorescence, ____________.
options: the main axis terminates in a flower
flowers are borne in an acropetal succession
questions.solution:
In racemose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow indefinitely and does not terminate in a flower. The flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal succession, meaning the older flowers are at the base and the younger flowers or buds are at the apex.

In cymose inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower, hence its growth is limited, and the flowers are borne in a basipetal order.

Answer: flowers are borne in an acropetal succession

B. AxileII. Pea
C. ParietalIII. Marigold

Marginal placentation is found in pea where the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary.

Axile placentation is found in lemon, tomato, and china rose where the placenta is axial and ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary.

Thus, A matches II, B matches IV, C matches I, and D matches III.

Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In angiosperms, root hairs arise from which one of the following regions of the root ?
questions.solution:
The root is divided into different regions from the apex to the base: the root cap, the region of meristematic activity, the region of elongation, and the region of maturation.

The cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature to form the region of maturation. From the epidermal cells of the region of maturation, very fine and delicate, thread-like structures called root hairs arise.

These root hairs significantly increase the surface area for the absorption of water and minerals from the soil.

Answer: The region of maturation

(b) Gulmohar

(c) Cassia

(d) Datura

(e) Chilly

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: In symmetry, the flower may be actinomorphic (radial symmetry) or zygomorphic (bilateral symmetry). When a flower can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through the centre, it is said to be actinomorphic, e.g., mustard, datura, chilli. When it can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane, it is zygomorphic, e.g., pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Which of the following floral formula is the correct floral formula of Solanaceae family ?
questions.solution:
The Solanaceae family exhibits the following floral characteristics:

- Symmetry: Actinomorphic, represented by $\oplus$.
- Sexuality: Bisexual.
- Calyx: 5 sepals that are united (gamosepalous), represented by $\text{K}_{(5)}$.
- Corolla: 5 petals that are united (gamopetalous), represented by $\text{C}_{(5)}$.
- Androecium: 5 stamens that are epipetalous (attached to the petals). This is represented by an arc connecting the corolla and androecium symbols: $\widehat{\text{C}_{(5)} \text{A}_{5}}$.
- Gynoecium: Bicarpellary, syncarpous, with a superior ovary, represented by $\underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}$.

Comparing these features with the given options, Formula (2) correctly displays all these characteristics. Formula (1) is incorrect as it lacks the arc indicating the epipetalous condition. Formulas (3) and (4) are incorrect because they show free sepals or petals (lacking parentheses).

Answer: Formula (2)

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: The roots that originate from the base of the stem are
questions.solution:
In the majority of dicot plants, the root system is formed by the direct elongation of the radicle into the primary root. Branches of the primary root are called secondary roots. These in turn branch to form tertiary roots. The primary root and its branches constitute the taproot system.

Prop roots: In trees like the banyan and Indian rubber plant, many adventitious roots arise from the horizontal branches of the stem and grow vertically downwards. They become thick pillar-like and provide mechanical support to the huge trees.

Stilt/Fibrous roots: These are small roots growing obliquely from the basal nodes of the main stem. Like prop roots, they also provide mechanical support.

questions.q: Pneumatophores occur in:
questions.solution:
Pneumatophores are extremely specialised aerial roots that stem out from a subterranean root system. They enable plants to utilise the air in waterlogged soil habitats. These roots are modified and show negative geotropism. These plants absorb oxygen from the air through their pneumatophores. The oxygen absorbed by the pneumatophores helps in the respiration of the underground tissues for their growth.

It is commonly found in mangrove species and are known as breathing roots.

questions.q: Sweet potato is a modified
questions.solution:
The sweet potato root system consists of fibrous roots - that absorb nutrients and water and anchor the plant and storage roots - which are lateral roots that store photosynthetic products.

The root system of sweet potato plants obtained by vegetative propagation starts with adventitious roots that develop into primary fibrous roots which branch into lateral roots. As the plant matures, thick pencil roots that become lignified are produced. Other roots without lignin, are fleshy and bulky and are called storage roots. Such roots are specialized to store food and get swollen in the process.

Plants are grown from true seed form a typical root system with a central axle with lateral branches. Later on, the central axle functions as a storage root.

questions.solution:
Technical terms used to describe a flower:
Incomplete: A flower is described as incomplete, if one or more whorls are absent. E.g. Euphorbia
Actinomorphic: If the flower can be divided into two equal halves from any plane of symmetry it is called an actinomorphic flower. E.g. members of Brassicaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae family.
Zygomorphic: If the flower can be divided into two equal parts by just one plane of symmetry it is called a zygomorphic flower. E.g. members of the Fabaceae family.
Asymmetric: When the flower cannot be divided into two equal halves by any plane of symmetry.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Which of the following is not a stem modification?
questions.solution: Pitcher of Nepenthes is a modification of the leaf. Nepenthes species usually produce two types of pitchers, known as leaf dimorphism. Appearing near the base of the plant are the large lower traps, which typically sit on the ground. The upper or aerial pitchers are usually smaller, coloured differently, and possess different features from the lower pitchers. These upper pitchers usually form as the plant reaches maturity and the plant grows taller. To keep the plant steady, the upper pitchers often form a loop in the tendril, allowing it to wrap around for nearby support.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: The hilum is a scar on the:
options: Fruit, where it was attached to pedicel
questions.solution:
Hilum is a scar on the surface of a seed marking its point of attachment to the seed stalk (funicle). Seed is developed from ovule and bears many structures that were present on the ovule.

Ovule is considered to be an integumented megasporangium. The ovule consists of the stalk and the body. The stalk is called funicle. One end of the funicle is attached to placenta and the other end to the body of the ovule. The point of attachment of funicle with the body is called hilum. Sometimes funicle gets fused with the body of the ovule one side and forms a ridge known as raphe. The body of the ovule shows two ends: the basal end, often called the chalazal end and the upper end is called micropylar end. The main body of the ovule is covered with one or two envelopes called integuments. These leave an opening at the top of the ovule called micropyle. The integuments enclose a large parenchymatous tissue known as nucellus.

questions.q: Non-albuminous seed is produced in:
questions.solution:
Albuminous seeds have stored food in a special type of nourishing tissue, endosperm. Endosperm remains persistent till maturity (germination) in these seeds. Examples - maize, wheat, and castor.

Non-albuminous seeds (also known as exalbuminous seeds) have stored food and cotyledons. In these seeds, the endosperm is completely used during the development of the embryo. Example - pea.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In a cymose inflorescence the main axis:
options: has unlimited growth but lateral branches end in flowers
questions.solution: In the cymose type of inflorescence, the main axis does not grow continuously. A flower is present terminally on the main axis. The flowers are borne in a basipetal order. The main axis has limited growth. The growth of the main axis is limited and the lateral axis also terminates into flower and that limits the growth of the axis. Flowers are present in the basipetal succession, i.e. older flower is present terminally and the younger ones at the base. This type of arrangement is known as centrifugal with the older flowers present in the middle and the younger ones at the periphery. In racemose types of inflorescence, the main axis grows continuously and flowers are present laterally on the floral axis. Flowers are present in an acropetal manner.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the main function of the primary root in dicotyledonous plants?
options: To absorb water and nutrients from the soil
To provide support to the stem
questions.solution: In monocotyledonous plants, the primary root is short lived and is replaced by a large number of roots. These roots originate from the base of the stem and constitute the fibrous root system, as seen in the wheat plant (Figure 5.2b). In some plants, like grass, Monstera and the banyan tree, roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle and are called adventitious roots (Figure 5.2c). The main functions of the root system are absorption of water and minerals from the soil, providing a proper anchorage to the plant parts, storing reserve food material and synthesis of plant growth regulators.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the purpose of the root cap in a plant root?
options: To protect the tender apex of the root
questions.solution: The root is covered at the apex by a thimble-like structure called the root cap (Figure 5.3). It protects the tender apex of the root as it makes its way through the soil. A few millimetres above the root cap is the region of meristematic activity. The cells of this region are very small, thin-walled and with dense protoplasm. They divide repeatedly. The cells proximal to this region undergo rapid elongation and enlargement and are responsible for the growth of the root in length. This region is called the region of elongation. The cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature. Hence, this zone, proximal to region of elongation, is called the region of maturation. From this region some of the epidermal cells form very fine and delicate, thread-like structures called root hairs. These root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil.

The cells proximal to this region undergo rapid elongation and enlargement and are responsible for the growth of the root in length. This region is called the region of elongation. The cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature. Hence, this zone, proximal to region of elongation, is called the region of maturation. questions.solution: The root is covered at the apex by a thimble-like structure called the root cap (Figure 5.3). It protects the tender apex of the root as it makes its way through the soil. A few millimetres above the root cap is the region of meristematic activity. The cells of this region are very small, thin-walled and with dense protoplasm. They divide repeatedly. The cells proximal to this region undergo rapid elongation and enlargement and are responsible for the growth of the root in length. This region is called the region of elongation. The cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature. Hence, this zone, proximal to region of elongation, is called the region of maturation. From this region some of the epidermal cells form very fine and delicate, thread-like structures called root hairs. These root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the main function of the stem?
questions.solution: The main function of the stem is spreading out branches bearing leaves, flowers and fruits. It conducts water, minerals and photosynthates. Some stems perform the function of storage of food, support, protection and of vegetative propagation.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the role of buds in the stem?
questions.solution: The leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem. It develops at the node and bears a bud in its axil. The axillary bud later develops into a branch. Leaves originate from shoot apical meristems and are arranged in an acropetal order. They are the most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What are the three main parts of a typical leaf?
options: Shoot apical meristems, acropetal order, and photosynthesis
questions.solution: A typical leaf consists of three main parts: leaf base, petiole and lamina (Figure 5.4 a). The leaf is attached to the stem by the leaf base and may bear two lateral small leaf like structures called stipules. In monocotyledons, the leaf base expands into a sheath covering the stem partially or wholly. In some leguminous plants the leafbase may become swollen, which is called the pulvinus. The petiole help hold the blade to light. Long thin flexible petioles allow leaf blades to flutter in wind, thereby cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to leaf surface. The lamina or the leaf blade is the green expanded part of the leaf with veins and veinlets. There is, usually, a middle prominent vein, which is known as the midrib. Veins provide rigidity to the leaf blade and act as channels of transport for water, minerals and food materials. The shape, margin, apex, surface and extent of incision of lamina varies in different leaves.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the term used to describe the arrangement of veins in the lamina of a leaf?
questions.solution: The arrangement of veins and the veinlets in the lamina of leaf is termed as venation. When the veinlets form a network, the venation is termed as reticulate (Figure 5.4 b). When the veins run parallel to each other within a lamina, the venation is termed as parallel (Figure 5.4 c). Leaves of dicotyledonous plants generally possess reticulate venation, while parallel venation is the characteristic of most monocotyledons.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the definition of a simple leaf?
options: A leaf with a divided lamina
A leaf with an undivided lamina
A leaf without a bud in the axil
questions.solution: A leaf is said to be simple, when its lamina is entire or when incised, the incisions do not touch the midrib. When the incisions of the lamina reach up to the midrib breaking it into a number of leaflets, the leaf is called compound. A bud is present in the axil of petiole in both simple and compound leaves, but not in the axil of leaflets of the compound leaf.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In which type of phyllotaxy does a single leaf arise at each node in an alternate manner?
questions.solution: Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. This is usually of three types – alternate, opposite and whorled (Figure 5.6). In alternate type of phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node in alternate manner, as in china rose, mustard and sun flower plants. In opposite type, a pair of leaves arise at each node and lie opposite to each other as in Calotropis and guava plants. If more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, it is called whorled, as in Alstonia.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is a flower?
questions.solution: A flower is a modified shoot wherein the shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem. Internodes do not elongate and the axis gets condensed. The apex produces different kinds of floral appendages laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves. When a shoot tip transforms into a flower, it is always solitary. The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is termed as inflorescence. Depending on whether the apex gets developed into a flower or continues to grow, two major types of inflorescences are defined – racemose and cymose.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What type of symmetry does a mustard flower have?
questions.solution: In symmetry, the flower may be actinomorphic (radial symmetry) or zygomorphic (bilateral symmetry). When a flower can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through the centre, it is said to be actinomorphic, e.g., mustard, datura, chilli. When it can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane, it is zygomorphic, e.g., pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia. A flower is asymmetric (irregular) if it cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre, as in canna.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What type of flower has the gynoecium occupying the highest position in relation to the ovary on the thalamus?
questions.solution: Based on the position of calyx, corolla and androecium in respect of the ovary on thalamus, the flowers are described as hypogynous,perigynous and epigynous (Figure 5.9). In the hypogynous flower the gynoecium occupies the highest position while the other parts are situated below it. The ovary in such flowers is said to be superior, e.g., mustard, china rose and brinjal.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the position of the ovary in perigynous flowers?
questions.solution: Based on the position of calyx, corolla and androecium in respect of the ovary on thalamus, the flowers are described as hypogynous, perigynous and epigynous (Figure 5.9). In the hypogynous flower the gynoecium occupies the highest position while the other parts are situated below it. The ovary in such flowers is said to be superior, e.g., mustard, china rose and brinjal. If gynoecium is situated in the centre and other parts of the flower are located on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level, it is called perigynous. The ovary here is said to be half inferior, e.g., plum, rose, peach. In epigynous flowers, the margin of thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely and getting fused with it, the other parts of flower arise above the ovary. Hence, the ovary is said to be inferior as in flowers of guava and cucumber, and the ray florets of sunflower.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the definition of aestivation?
options: The study of plants and flowers
The study of birds and their habitats
The arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl
questions.solution: The mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl is known as aestivation. The main types of aestivation are valvate, twisted, imbricate and vexillary (Figure 5.11). When sepals or petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margin, without overlapping, as in Calotropis, it is said to be valvate. If one margin of the appendage overlaps that of the next one and so on as in china rose, lady’s finger and cotton, it is called twisted. If the margins of sepals or petals overlap one another but not in any particular direction as in Cassia and gulmohur, the aestivation is called imbricate. In pea and bean flowers, there are five petals, the largest (standard) overlaps the two lateral petals (wings) which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel); this type of aestivation is known as vexillary or papilionaceous.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the structure of a stamen in the androecium?
questions.solution: Androecium is composed of stamens. Each stamen which represents the male reproductive organ consists of a stalk or a filament and an anther. Each anther is usually bilobed and each lobe has two chambers, the pollen-sacs. The pollen grains are produced in pollen-sacs. A sterile stamen is called staminode.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What are stamens attached to the other members of a flower?
questions.solution: Stamens of flower may be united with other members such as petals or among themselves. When stamens are attached to the petals, they are epipetalous as in brinjal, or epiphyllous when attached to the perianth as in the flowers of lily. The stamens in a flower may either remain free (polyandrous) or may be united in varying degrees. The stamens may be united into one bunch or one bundle (monoadelphous) as in china rose, or two bundles (diadelphous) as in pea, or into more than two bundles (polyadelphous) as in citrus. There may be a variation in the length of filaments within a flower, as in Salvia and mustard.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the function of the stigma in the female reproductive part of a flower?
options: To connect the ovary to the style
questions.solution: Gynoecium is the female reproductive part of the flower and is made up of one or more carpels. A carpel consists of three parts namely stigma, style and ovary. Ovary is the enlarged basal part, on which lies the elongated tube, the style. The style connects the ovary to the stigma. The stigma is usually at the tip of the style and is the receptive surface for pollen grains. Each ovary bears one or more ovules attached to a flattened, cushion-like placenta. When more than one carpel is present, they may be free (as in lotus and rose) and are called apocarpous. They are termed syncarpous when carpels are fused, as in mustard and tomato. After fertilisation, the ovules develop into seeds and the ovary matures into a fruit.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In which type of placentation do the ovules form a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary?
questions.solution: The arrangement of ovules within the ovary is known as placentation. The placentation are of different types namely, marginal, axile, parietal, basal, central and free central (Figure 5.12). In marginal placentation the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and the ovules are borne on this ridge forming two rows, as in pea. When the placenta is axial and the ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary, the placentaion is said to be axile, as in china rose, tomato and lemon. In parietal placentation, the ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on peripheral part. Ovary is one-chambered but it becomes twochambered due to the formation of the false septum, e.g., mustard and Argemone. When the ovules are borne on central axis and septa are absent, as in Dianthus and Primrose the placentation is called free central. In basal placentation, the placenta develops at the base of ovary and a single ovule is attached to it, as in sunflower, marigold.

questions.solution:
Explanation : The fruit is a characteristic feature of the flowering plants. It is a mature or ripened ovary, developed after fertilisation. If a fruit is formed without fertilisation of the ovary, it is called a parthenocarpic fruit.

In mango and coconut, the fruit is known as a drupe (Figure

5.13). They develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are

one seeded.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the difference between mango and coconut as a drupe?
options: Mango is one seeded while coconut is not
Coconut is well differentiated while mango is not
Mango has a stony endocarp while coconut does not
Coconut has an edible mesocarp while mango does not
questions.solution: In mango and coconut, the fruit is known as a drupe (Figure 5.13). They develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one seeded. In mango the pericarp is well differentiated into an outer thin epicarp, a middle fleshy edible mesocarp and an inner stony hard endocarp. In coconut which is also a drupe, the mesocarp is fibrous.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the outermost covering of a seed called?
questions.solution: The outermost covering of a seed is the seed coat. The seed coat has two layers, the outer testa and the inner tegmen. The hilum is a scar on the seed coat through which the developing seeds were attached to the fruit.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What are the two parts of the embryo in a seed?
questions.solution: Above the hilum is a small pore called the micropyle. Within the seed coat is the embryo, consisting of an embryonal axis and two cotyledons. The cotyledons are often fleshy and full of reserve food materials. At the two ends of the embryonal axis are present the radicle and the plumule.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What is the difference between endospermic and non endospermic seeds?
options: Endospermic seeds have endosperm while non endospermic seeds do not
Endospermic seeds have a larger hilum than non endospermic seeds
Endospermic seeds have a larger embryo than non endospermic seeds
Endospermic seeds are more mature than non endospermic seeds
questions.solution: In some seeds such as castor the endosperm formed as a result of double fertilisation, is a food storing tissue and called endospermic seeds. In plants such as bean, gram and pea, the endosperm is not present in mature seeds and such seeds are called non-endospermous.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: What type of seed is found in cereal plants such as maize?
questions.solution: Generally, monocotyledonous seeds are endospermic but some as in orchids are non-endospermic. In the seeds of cereals such as maize the seed coat is membranous and generally fused with the fruit wall.The endosperm is bulky and stores food. The outer covering of endosperm separates the embryo by a proteinous layer called aleurone layer. The embryo is small and situated in a groove at one end of the endosperm. It consists of one large and shield shaped cotyledon known as scutellum and a short axis with a plumule and a radicle. The plumule and radicle are enclosed in sheaths which are called coleoptile and coleorhiza respectively.

(a)E-Stipules: The lateral small leaf-like structures. (b)A-Leaf base: The leaf is attached to the stem by the leaf base (c)D-Axillary bud: It later develops into a branch. (d)E-Petiole: The petiole helps hold the lamina to light. (e)B-Axillary bud: It later develops into a branch. (f)C-Petiole: The petiole helps hold the lamina to light. (g)D-Leaf base: The leaf is attached to the stem by the leaf base. (h)A-Leaf blade: It is the green expanded part of the leaf with veins and veinlets. questions.solution: A typical leaf consists of three main parts: leaf base, petiole and lamina (Figure 5.4 a). The leaf is attached to the stem by the leaf base and may bear two lateral small leaf-like structures called stipules. The petiole helps hold the blade to light. Long thin flexible petioles allow leaf blades to flutter in the wind, thereby cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to leaf surface.The lamina or the leaf blade is the green expanded part of the leaf with veins and veinlets.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q:
Match the type of placentation in Column I with its corresponding structural characteristic and plant example in Column II.
Column IColumn II
(a) Axile(i) False septum formation in a unilocular ovary; Mustard
(b) Parietal(ii) Single ovule attached at the ovary base; Sunflower
(c) Free central(iii) Multilocular ovary with central attachment; Lemon
(d) Basal(iv) Septa are completely absent; Dianthus
Select the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.solution:
Refer: NCERT | Class 11 | Page: 65 | Paragraph: 2

Axile placentation occurs in a multilocular ovary where ovules are attached to the central axis. Example: Lemon. Thus, (a) matches (iii).

Parietal placentation occurs when ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary. A false septum may form, making the unilocular ovary bilocular. Example: Mustard. Thus, (b) matches (i).

Free central placentation features ovules borne on a central axis with septa completely absent. Example: Dianthus. Thus, (c) matches (iv).

Basal placentation involves a single ovule attached at the base of the ovary. Example: Sunflower. Thus, (d) matches (ii).

The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

Answer: (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii)

questions.q:
Read the following list of plants:
Mustard, Brinjal, China rose, Plum, Rose, Peach, Guava, Cucumber, Ray florets of sunflower

How many of the given plants have a superior ovary?
questions.solution:
Based on the position of calyx, corolla and androecium in respect of the ovary on the thalamus, flowers are described as hypogynous, perigynous and epigynous.

In a hypogynous flower, the gynoecium occupies the highest position while the other parts are situated below it. The ovary in such flowers is said to be superior. Examples include mustard, china rose and brinjal.

In perigynous flowers, the ovary is half inferior. Examples include plum, rose and peach.

In epigynous flowers, the ovary is inferior. Examples include guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower.

Therefore, out of the 9 given plants, exactly 3 (mustard, brinjal, and china rose) have a superior ovary.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Which of the following morphological features is shared by both a mature maize grain and a mature castor seed?
options: Presence of a coleoptile protecting the shoot apex
Fused seed coat and fruit wall
questions.solution:
Maize is a monocotyledonous plant and its grain is typically endospermic. Castor is a dicotyledonous plant, but unlike many dicots (such as pea or gram), it is an exception and has endospermic seeds.

Therefore, the presence of a bulky endosperm is a feature shared by both mature maize and castor seeds.

Maize has a single cotyledon (scutellum) and a fused seed coat and fruit wall, whereas castor has two cotyledons and a distinct seed coat. A coleoptile is found only in monocots like maize.

Answer: Presence of a bulky endosperm

The morphological features described in the question, such as a membranous seed coat fused with the fruit wall, a bulky endosperm, and a proteinous aleurone layer separating the embryo, are characteristic of monocotyledonous endospermic seeds of cereals like maize.

Castor is incorrect because it is a dicotyledonous endospermic seed and its seed coat is not fused with the fruit wall. Orchid is incorrect because, although it is a monocot, it produces non-endospermic seeds. Gram is incorrect as it is a dicotyledonous non-endospermic seed.

Answer: Maize

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Identify the incorrect statement regarding the morphological modifications in plants:
options: In watermelon and grapevine, leaves are modified into long, slender and coiled tendrils to help them climb.
In Australian acacia, the leaves are small and short-lived, so the petioles expand, become green and synthesise food.
The fleshy leaves of onion and garlic are modified to store food.
Pitcher plant and Venus-fly trap are examples of plants possessing modified leaves.
questions.solution:
The statement regarding watermelon and grapevine is incorrect. In gourds (like cucumber, pumpkins, watermelon) and grapevines, it is the stem (specifically the axillary bud) that is modified into slender and spirally coiled tendrils to help the plant climb, not the leaves. Leaf tendrils are found in plants like peas.

The other statements are correct facts from NCERT: the fleshy leaves of onion and garlic store food; in Australian acacia, the petioles expand to become green and synthesise food (a modification known as a phyllode); and the insect-catching structures of pitcher plant and Venus-fly trap are modified leaves.

Answer: In watermelon and grapevine, leaves are modified into long, slender and coiled tendrils to help them climb.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: A flower is observed to have vexillary aestivation in its corolla. Which of the following combinations of floral symmetry and placentation is most likely to be found in this flower?
questions.solution:
Vexillary aestivation is a characteristic feature of the family Fabaceae (e.g., pea, bean).

Flowers belonging to the family Fabaceae exhibit zygomorphic (bilateral) symmetry. Their gynoecium consists of a monocarpellary, unilocular ovary with marginal placentation.

Actinomorphic symmetry and axile placentation are typically seen in families like Solanaceae and Liliaceae, which do not show vexillary aestivation.

Answer: Zygomorphic symmetry and marginal placentation

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: While studying the floral morphology of angiosperms, a student compares the families Fabaceae, Solanaceae, and Liliaceae. Which of the following gynoecium characteristics is exclusively found in family Liliaceae among the three?
options: Bicarpellary, syncarpous ovary with swollen placenta
Tricarpellary, syncarpous ovary with axile placentation
Monocarpellary, superior ovary with marginal placentation
Tricarpellary, apocarpous ovary with parietal placentation
questions.solution:
According to NCERT, the gynoecium of family Liliaceae is tricarpellary, syncarpous with a superior ovary and axile placentation.

Family Fabaceae has a monocarpellary, superior ovary with marginal placentation.

Family Solanaceae has a bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary with axile placentation and a characteristic swollen placenta.

Therefore, the tricarpellary, syncarpous condition is specific to Liliaceae among the three families. The option stating apocarpous and parietal placentation is incorrect for Liliaceae.

Answer: Tricarpellary, syncarpous ovary with axile placentation

Answer: Tricarpellary, syncarpous ovary with axile placentation

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Which of the following flowers cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre?
questions.solution:
According to NCERT, a flower is asymmetric (irregular) if it cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre. Canna is the classic example of an asymmetric flower.

Mustard and Datura exhibit actinomorphic (radial) symmetry, meaning they can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through the centre. Gulmohur exhibits zygomorphic (bilateral) symmetry, meaning it can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane.

Answer: Canna

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q:
Read the following statements regarding the androecium in different plants:

(I) In China rose, stamens are united into one bunch (monadelphous).
(II) In pea, stamens are united into two bundles (diadelphous).
(III) In Citrus, stamens are united into more than two bundles (polyadelphous).
(IV) In lily, stamens are attached to the petals (epipetalous).

Choose the correct combination of statements.
questions.solution:
Statement (I) is correct: In China rose, the stamens are united into a single bundle, which is termed monadelphous.

Statement (II) is correct: In pea, the stamens are united into two bundles, termed diadelphous.

Statement (III) is correct: In Citrus, the stamens are united into more than two bundles, termed polyadelphous.

Statement (IV) is incorrect: In lily, the stamens are attached to the perianth, a condition known as epiphyllous, not epipetalous. Epipetalous condition (attachment to petals) is seen in brinjal.

Therefore, only statements (I), (II) and (III) are correct.

Answer: Only (I), (II) and (III) are correct

questions.q: Identify the correct combination of the state of carpel fusion, type of placentation, and the corresponding plant example.
questions.solution:
Tomato has a syncarpous gynoecium (carpels are fused) and exhibits axile placentation, where the placenta is axial and ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary.

Rose and lotus have an apocarpous gynoecium (carpels are free).

Argemone also has a syncarpous gynoecium (not apocarpous) and exhibits parietal placentation.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Which of the following plants possesses an inferior ovary?
questions.solution:
In epigynous flowers, the margin of the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely and getting fused with it, while the other parts of the flower arise above the ovary. Hence, the ovary is said to be inferior.

Examples of plants with epigynous flowers (inferior ovary) include guava, cucumber, and the ray florets of sunflower.

Brinjal and mustard have hypogynous flowers with a superior ovary, whereas peach has a perigynous flower with a half-inferior ovary.

Answer: Cucumber

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Which of the following plants exhibits twisted aestivation in its corolla and axile placentation in its ovary?
questions.solution:
Twisted aestivation is seen in plants where one margin of the appendage overlaps that of the next one, and so on. Examples include China rose, lady's finger, and cotton.

Axile placentation occurs when the placenta is axial and the ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary. Examples include China rose, tomato, and lemon.

Therefore, China rose exhibits both twisted aestivation and axile placentation.

Pea has vexillary aestivation and marginal placentation. Tomato has valvate aestivation and axile placentation. Cassia has imbricate aestivation and marginal placentation.

Answer: China rose

questions.q:
Read the following statements regarding the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis:
(A) In racemose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow indefinitely.
(B) In cymose inflorescence, flowers are borne in an acropetal succession.
(C) In racemose inflorescence, flowers are borne laterally.
(D) In cymose inflorescence, the main axis has unlimited growth.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct: In racemose inflorescences, the main axis does not terminate in a flower and continues to grow.

Statement (B) is incorrect: In cymose inflorescence, flowers are borne in a basipetal order, whereas acropetal succession is a feature of racemose inflorescence.

Statement (C) is correct: In racemose inflorescence, the flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal succession.

Statement (D) is incorrect: In cymose inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower, hence its growth is limited.

Therefore, exactly two statements, (A) and (C), are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the arrangement of ovules within the ovary in plants like sunflower and marigold?
options: The placenta is axial and ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary.
The placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it.
The ovules are borne on the central axis and septa are absent.
The placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and ovules are borne on this ridge.
questions.solution:
Sunflower and marigold exhibit basal placentation. In basal placentation, the placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it.

The placenta being axial in a multilocular ovary describes axile placentation (e.g., tomato). Ovules borne on a central axis without septa describes free central placentation (e.g., Primrose). A placenta forming a ridge along the ventral suture describes marginal placentation (e.g., pea).

Answer: The placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it.

The placenta being axial in a multilocular ovary describes axile placentation (e.g., tomato). Ovules borne on a central axis without septa describes free central placentation (e.g., Primrose). A placenta forming a ridge along the ventral suture describes marginal placentation (e.g., pea).

Answer: The placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In a certain plant, a pair of leaves arise at each node and lie opposite to each other. Which of the following plants exhibits this type of leaf arrangement?
questions.solution:
The arrangement where a pair of leaves arise at each node and lie opposite to each other is defined as opposite phyllotaxy.

According to NCERT, Calotropis and guava plants exhibit opposite phyllotaxy.

Alstonia shows whorled phyllotaxy (more than two leaves arise at a node). Mustard and sunflower show alternate phyllotaxy (a single leaf arises at each node in an alternate manner).

Answer: Calotropis

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q:
Observe the following floral formula of a plant family (the symbol for sexuality is omitted):

$\oplus \text{ } \text{K}_{(5)} \text{ } \overset{\frown}{\text{C}_{(5)} \text{A}_{5}} \text{ } \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}$

Read the following statements regarding the morphology of the flower based on this formula:
(A) The flower exhibits actinomorphic symmetry.
(B) The stamens are attached to the perianth, showing an epiphyllous condition.
(C) The gynoecium consists of a superior ovary.
(D) The sepals are free from one another.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
The given floral formula represents the family Solanaceae.

Statement (A) is correct: The symbol $\oplus$ indicates that the flower is actinomorphic (radial symmetry).

Statement (B) is incorrect: The arc over $\text{C}_{(5)}$ and $\text{A}_{5}$ ($\overset{\frown}{\text{C}_{(5)} \text{A}_{5}}$) indicates that the stamens are attached to the petals, which is the epipetalous condition. The epiphyllous condition involves attachment to the perianth ($\text{P}$).

Statement (C) is correct: The line below $\text{G}$ ($\underline{\text{G}}$) indicates a superior ovary.

Statement (D) is incorrect: The brackets around the number of sepals in $\text{K}_{(5)}$ indicate that the sepals are fused (gamosepalous condition), not free.

Therefore, exactly two statements ((A) and (C)) are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.solution:
The given description refers to vexillary (or papilionaceous) aestivation, where the largest petal (standard) overlaps the two lateral petals (wings), which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel).

Cassia exhibits imbricate aestivation. Calotropis exhibits valvate aestivation. Cotton exhibits twisted aestivation.

Answer: Bean

questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true because Alstonia is a classic example of whorled phyllotaxy.

Reason (R) is false because the statement describes opposite phyllotaxy (where a pair of leaves arise at each node and lie opposite to each other, as seen in Calotropis and guava). In whorled phyllotaxy, more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl.

Therefore, (A) is true but (R) is false.

questions.q:

Assertion (A): The flower of mustard is described as epigynous.
Reason (R): In mustard flowers, the gynoecium occupies the highest position while the other floral parts are situated below it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
The Assertion (A) is not correct because the flower of mustard is an example of a hypogynous flower, not an epigynous one. In epigynous flowers, the margin of the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely.

The Reason (R) is correct because it accurately describes the arrangement of floral parts in mustard. In mustard (a hypogynous flower), the gynoecium occupies the highest position on the thalamus while the calyx, corolla, and androecium are situated below it, making the ovary superior.

Answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct

Therefore, Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

Assertion (A): In a cymose inflorescence, the youngest flowers or buds are present at the apex of the main axis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
The Assertion (A) is not correct. In a cymose inflorescence, the flowers are borne in a basipetal order. This means that the oldest flower is present at the apex and the younger flowers or buds are present towards the base.

The Reason (R) is correct. The main axis in a cymose inflorescence terminates in a flower, which limits its further growth. This early termination of the main axis is the reason why subsequent younger flowers arise laterally below it, resulting in the basipetal succession.

Answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct

Read the following statements regarding seed structures:
(A) Scutellum is the large and shield-shaped cotyledon found in the seeds of grasses.
(B) Epiblast represents the persistent endosperm in mature seeds.
(C) Perisperm is the residual, persistent nucellus found in seeds like black pepper.
(D) Groundnut and pea are examples of albuminous seeds.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct as the single cotyledon of monocots (like grasses) is called the scutellum.

Statement (B) is incorrect because the epiblast is a rudimentary second cotyledon present in some grass embryos, not persistent endosperm.

Statement (C) is correct as the residual, persistent nucellus in seeds like black pepper and beet is called perisperm.

Statement (D) is incorrect because groundnut and pea are non-albuminous (non-endospermic) seeds, as their endosperm is completely consumed during embryo development.

Thus, exactly two statements (A and C) are correct.

Answer: Only two

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q:
Read the following statements carefully:
(A) In Calotropis, sepals or petals just touch one another at the margin, without overlapping.
(B) In Lady's finger, one margin of the appendage overlaps that of the next one and so on.
(C) In Gulmohur, the margins of sepals or petals overlap one another in a particular direction.
(D) In Bean flowers, the two smallest anterior petals overlap the lateral petals.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct. In Calotropis, the aestivation is valvate, where sepals or petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margin, without overlapping.

Statement (B) is correct. In Lady's finger, the aestivation is twisted, where one margin of the appendage overlaps that of the next one and so on.

Statement (C) is incorrect. In Gulmohur, the aestivation is imbricate. The margins of sepals or petals overlap one another but not in any particular direction.

Statement (D) is incorrect. In Bean flowers, the aestivation is vexillary. The largest petal (standard) overlaps the two lateral petals (wings), which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel). Therefore, the anterior petals are overlapped by the lateral petals, not the other way around.

Thus, exactly two statements are correct.

Answer: Only two

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In a mature seed of black pepper, what is the correct sequence of ploidy levels for its perisperm, endosperm, and cotyledon respectively?
questions.solution:
In black pepper, the perisperm represents the persistent nucellus. Since the nucellus is a maternal sporophytic tissue, it is diploid ($2n$).

The endosperm in angiosperms is formed by the primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) via triple fusion, making it triploid ($3n$).

The cotyledon is a part of the embryo, which develops from the zygote formed by syngamy, making it diploid ($2n$).

Therefore, the correct sequence of ploidy levels is $2n, 3n, 2n$.

Answer: $2n, 3n, 2n$

questions.q: Which of the following is the defining characteristic of the root region situated immediately proximal to the region of elongation?
options: The cells are very small, thin-walled and possess dense protoplasm.

The presence of a multicellular, thimble-like structure that protects the tender apex.
The cells gradually differentiate and mature, with some epidermal cells forming delicate thread-like structures.
questions.solution:
The root tip is divided into four regions from apex to base: root cap, region of meristematic activity, region of elongation, and region of maturation.

The region situated immediately proximal to (above) the region of elongation is the region of maturation. In this zone, cells gradually differentiate and mature. Additionally, some of the epidermal cells from this region form very fine and delicate, thread-like structures called root hairs.

The cells that are small, thin-walled and have dense protoplasm belong to the region of meristematic activity. The cells undergoing rapid enlargement belong to the region of elongation. The thimble-like structure is the root cap.

Answer: The cells gradually differentiate and mature, with some epidermal cells forming delicate thread-like structures.

Thus, the correct sequence is Superior, Half-inferior, Inferior.

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II)

Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
According to NCERT, the root is divided into different regions from the apex to the base. The cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature to form the region of maturation. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are true statements, and the Reason correctly explains why root hairs are found in the maturation zone rather than in the meristematic or elongation zones.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q:
Read the following statements carefully regarding the regions of the root:

Statement A: The region of meristematic activity is situated distal to the region of elongation.
Statement B: Cells of the elongation zone undergo rapid elongation and enlargement.
Statement C: Root hairs are multicellular epidermal structures arising from the maturation zone.
Statement D: The root cap is a thimble-like structure that protects the tender apex of the root.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement A is correct: The region of elongation is proximal to the meristematic zone, which means the meristematic zone is distal (towards the tip) to the elongation zone.

Statement B is correct: The cells of the elongation zone undergo rapid elongation and enlargement, being responsible for the growth of the root in length.

Statement C is incorrect: Root hairs do arise from the maturation zone, but they are unicellular elongations of the epidermal cells, not multicellular. Multicellular epidermal hairs are typically trichomes found on the shoot system.

Statement D is correct: The root cap is a thimble-like structure covering the root apex to protect it as it penetrates the soil.

Therefore, exactly three statements (A, B, and D) are correct.

Answer: Only three

questions.solution:
According to NCERT, in valvate aestivation, sepals or petals just touch one another at the margin without overlapping (e.g., Calotropis).

In twisted aestivation, one margin of the appendage overlaps that of the next one (e.g., cotton).

In imbricate aestivation, margins overlap but not in any particular direction (e.g., gulmohur).

In vexillary aestivation, the largest petal overlaps the two lateral petals, which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals (e.g., bean).

Therefore, the correct match is (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)

questions.solution:
In the Lily family (Liliaceae), the calyx and corolla are not distinct and are collectively termed as the perianth, represented by the symbol $\text{P}$.

The stamens (androecium, $\text{A}$) are attached to the perianth, which is known as the epiphyllous or epitepalous condition. This adhesion is represented by an arc drawn above the symbols of perianth and androecium ($\widehat{\text{P A}}$). Therefore, Assertion (A) is true.

Reason (R) is false because the flowers of the Lily family exhibit an epiphyllous condition, not an epipetalous condition. Epipetalous condition means stamens are attached to petals (represented by $\widehat{\text{C A}}$), which is seen in plants like Solanum, not Lily.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false

Answer: Parallel venation

The arc over $\mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{A}$ ($\widehat{\mathrm{C}_{(5)} \mathrm{A}}_{5}$) indicates that the stamens are attached to the petals, which is the epipetalous condition.

The underline beneath $\mathrm{G}$ ($\underline{\mathrm{G}}_{(2)}$) indicates a superior ovary. Flowers with a superior ovary are termed hypogynous.

Therefore, the correct set of terms is Actinomorphic, epipetalous, hypogynous.

Answer: Actinomorphic, epipetalous, hypogynous

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Select the pair that correctly represents a non-endospermic monocot seed and an endospermic dicot seed, respectively.
questions.solution:
Generally, monocotyledonous seeds are endospermic (albuminous) and dicotyledonous seeds are non-endospermic (exalbuminous).

However, orchids are an exception among monocots as they have non-endospermic seeds.

Castor is an exception among dicots as it has endospermic seeds.

Wheat and maize are typical endospermic monocots, while gram and pea are typical non-endospermic dicots.

Therefore, the correct pair representing a non-endospermic monocot and an endospermic dicot respectively is Orchid and Castor.

Answer: Orchid and Castor

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the position of floral parts on the thalamus and select the correct option.

List-I (Flower type)List-II (Example)
A. HypogynousI. Rose
B. PerigynousII. Guava
C. EpigynousIII. Brinjal
questions.solution:
Based on the position of calyx, corolla, and androecium in respect of the ovary on the thalamus, flowers are described as hypogynous, perigynous, and epigynous.

A. Hypogynous flower: The gynoecium occupies the highest position while the other parts are situated below it. The ovary is superior. Examples: mustard, china rose, and brinjal. (A matches III)

B. Perigynous flower: The gynoecium is situated in the centre and other parts of the flower are located on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level. The ovary is half-inferior. Examples: plum, rose, and peach. (B matches I)

C. Epigynous flower: The margin of the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely and getting fused with it, and the other parts of the flower arise above the ovary. The ovary is inferior. Examples: guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower. (C matches II)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-III, B-I, C-II.

Answer: A-III, B-I, C-II

questions.q: In a particular type of inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower, hence its growth is limited. This type of arrangement is termed as:
questions.solution:
According to NCERT, in the cymose type of inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower, which results in its limited growth. The flowers in this type are borne in a basipetal order.

In contrast, the racemose inflorescence features a main axis that continues to grow indefinitely. Solitary axillary refers to a single flower in the axil of a leaf, and actinomorphic is a term used for radial symmetry in flowers, not an inflorescence type.

Answer: Cymose

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The root apex consists of different zones with specific characteristics.

The root cap (A) is a thimble-like structure that protects the tender apex of the root (IV).

The region of meristematic activity (B) is located a few millimetres above the root cap. Its cells are very small, thin-walled, and with dense protoplasm (I).

The region of elongation (C) is proximal to the meristematic region, where cells undergo rapid elongation and enlargement (II).

The region of maturation (D) is proximal to the elongation zone, where cells differentiate and mature, and epidermal cells form delicate thread-like structures called root hairs (III).

Therefore, the correct match is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

Answer: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: Which of the following represents the correct floral formula for Pisum sativum?
questions.solution:
Pisum sativum (garden pea) belongs to the family Fabaceae.

The flowers of Fabaceae are zygomorphic ($\text{\%}$) and bisexual.

The calyx consists of 5 united sepals ($\text{K}_{(5)}$).

The corolla is papilionaceous, consisting of 5 petals: 1 standard, 2 wings, and 2 fused keel petals ($\text{C}_{1+2+(2)}$).

The androecium consists of 10 stamens which are diadelphous ($\text{A}_{(9)+1}$).

The gynoecium is monocarpellary with a superior ovary ($\underline{\text{G}}_{1}$).

Therefore, the correct floral formula is $\%$, Bisexual, $\text{K}_{(5)}\ \text{C}_{1+2+(2)}\ \text{A}_{(9)+1}\ \underline{\text{G}}_{1}$.

Answer: $\%$, Bisexual, $\text{K}_{(5)}\ \text{C}_{1+2+(2)}\ \text{A}_{(9)+1}\ \underline{\text{G}}_{1}$

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the structure of a monocotyledonous seed.

List-IList-II
A. Aleurone layerI. Shield shaped cotyledon
B. ScutellumII. Proteinaceous covering of endosperm
C. ColeoptileIII. Sheath enclosing radicle
D. ColeorhizaIV. Sheath enclosing plumule

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
In a monocotyledonous seed (like maize), the outer covering of endosperm separates the embryo by a proteinaceous layer called the aleurone layer (A-II).

The embryo consists of one large and shield-shaped cotyledon known as scutellum (B-I).

The plumule and radicle are enclosed in sheaths which are called coleoptile (C-IV) and coleorhiza (D-III) respectively.

Answer: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In unilocular ovary with a single ovule, the placentation is
questions.solution:
In basal placentation, ovary is bicarpellary, syncarpous and unilocular and a single ovule is borne at the base of ovary, eg, marigold.
In marginal placentation, the ovary is simple, unilocular and the ovules are arranged along the margin of the unilocular ovary, eg, pea.
In free central placentation, ovary is unilocular and the placenta bearing ovules are arised from the central axis, eg, Stellaria.
In axile placentation, ovary is two or more chambered, usually as many as the number of carpels, eg, Petunia.

In axile placentation, ovary is two or more chambered, usually as many as the number of carpels, eg, Petunia.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: The ability of the Venus fly trap to capture insects is due to:
options: a passive process requiring no special ability on the part of the plant
questions.solution:
When a fly sits on the leaf of venus fly trap, there are touch-sensitive hairs that trigger an electrical potential. This potential cause several changes which result in the movement of ions inside the cells of the leaf. Inflow of water in the cells follows which results in their becoming turgid. This causes the shutting of the trap.
Related Theory
The Venus fly trap is a carnivorous flowering plant. The trap is made of two hinged lobes at the end of each leaf. On the inner surfaces of the lobes are hair-like projections called trichomes that cause the lobes to snap shut when prey comes in contact with them (thigmonastic movement).

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: In a longitudinal section of a root. Starting from the tip upward the four zones occur in the following order:
options: rootcap, cell division, cellenlargement, cell maturation
root cap, cell division, cell maturation, cell enlargement
cell division, cell enlargement, cell maturation, root cap
cell division, cell maturation, cell enlargement, root cap.
questions.solution:
The root tip can be divided into three zones: a zone of cell division, a zone of elongation, and a zone of maturation. The zone of cell division is closest to the root tip and is made up of the actively-dividing cells of the root meristem, which contains the undifferentiated cells of the germinating plant. The zone of elongation is where the newlyformed cells increase in length, thereby lengthening the root. zone of cell maturation where the root cells differentiate into specialized cell types.
Related Theory Root growth begins with seed germination. When the plant embryo emerges from the seed, the radicle of the embryo forms the root system. The tip of the root is protected by the root cap, a structure exclusive to roots and unlike any other plant structure. The root cap is continuously replaced because it is easily damaged as the root pushes through soil.

questions.solution:

Related Theory
If the apical meristem is removed by removing the end of the stem, the lateral buds will be released from apical dominance, and greater branching results. Eventually, one of the lateral meristems will grow more than the others and will impose apical dominance, becoming the new apical meristem.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: The cells of the quiescent centre are characterised by
options: having dense cytoplasm and prominent nuclei
having light cytoplasm and small nuclei
dividing regularly to add to the corpus
dividing regularly to add to tunica
questions.solution: In the apices of some roots, (e.g., Zea mays, maize), there is a central region of cells which normally does not divide. This central inactive region was called quiescent centre by F.A.L. Clowes $(1959,1961)$. The cells of this region have lesser amounts of RNA and DNA so they have small nuclei. These cells also have a lower rate of protein synthesis. Mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum are less developed. The cells of the quiescent centre are usually inactive. However, if already existing meristematic cells are injured or become inactive due to any other reason, the cells of quiescent centre become active.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q:
Assertion : Nuclear endosperm is formed by subsequent nuclear division without wall formation.
Reason : Coconut is an example of such endosperm, where the endosperm remains nuclear throughout the development of the fruit.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
If assertion is true but reason is false
If both assertion and reason are false.
questions.solution: In nuclear endosperm, first and further divisions of primary endosperm nucleus are not followed by cytokinesis or wall formation and thus these free nuclear divisions lead to formation of a large number of free nuclei in embryo sac. At maturity, centripetal wall formation may occur to make the tissue partly cellular. Endosperm of coconut is unique in sense that it is both nuclear and cellular. Here the primary endosperm nucleus undergoes a number of free nuclear divisions. When the fruit is about $50 \mathrm{~mm}$ long the embryo sac remains filled with a watery fluid or milk containing free nuclei and fine cytoplasmic particles. At a later stage when the fruit becomes about $100 \mathrm{~mm}$ in length the liquid shows in addition to free nuclei, several cells each enclosing variable number of nuclei. Thus coconut has multicellular endosperm (called coconut meat) in the outer part and free nuclear as well as vacuolate endosperm (called coconut milk) in the centre.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.q: The ability of the venus flytrap to capture insects is due to
options: a passive process requiring no special ability on the part of the plant
questions.solution: Insectivorous plants grow in water logged swampy soils, deficient in nitrogenous compounds. These plants obtain their nitrogen compounds from the insects. Due to this reason, these plants are called as semi-autotrophic or semi-heterotrophic. Dionea (an insectivorous plant) is commonly called as venus fly trap. Leaves of this plant have winged petiole and lamina modified into two toothed jaws. Each jaw bears several teeth. Upper surface of each jaw bears triangularly arranged long sensitive hairs or bristles and many glands, which are irregularly scattered. These hairs are very sensitive to touch stimulus. When an insect touches these hairs, this stimulus causes rapid turgor pressure changes which closes the leaf.
